items.title: Coding Agent Memory Gets Its Own Benchmark: Devin Leads, but a Plugin Reorders the Board
items.summary: past.dev replayed 13,539 dated messages from three simulated people (~500k tokens each) into Devin, Claude Code and Codex, let each build its own long-term memory, then ran all three on the same 600 DolphinBench tasks in fresh conversations. Built-in memory scored Devin Memory 84.7% (508/600), Claude Code auto memory 76.2% and Codex Memory v2 66.3%. Adding past.dev's recall plugin lifted them to 93.2%, 89.7% and 85.8% respectively - a 19.5-point jump for Codex - and cut Claude Code's cost per passed task from $0.449 to $0.264. The designs differ sharply: Devin stores one-line lessons in a personal Git Memory Drive, each linked to its source session, and runs a daily 'Dreaming' pass to merge stale notes; Claude Code uses a MEMORY.md index plus topic files; Codex consolidates idle threads in the background; Copilot stores repository facts server-side with 90-day expiry. Cognition has open-sourced the Git format as Agent Memory Repo under MIT.
items.impact: Memory is becoming a first-class, measurable subsystem of coding agents rather than a prompt trick - and the vendor-run results suggest built-in memory is still beatable by a recall layer. The practical takeaway for teams is to treat memory as versioned infrastructure with consolidation, provenance and off-switches. Caveat: past.dev sells one of the options tested, ran the benchmark itself, and used a different model in each harness, so the numbers are not comparable with DolphinBench's public leaderboard.

items.title: Coding Agents Beat Video Models at Visual Reasoning - by Writing Code
items.summary: A multi-university paper tested a simple premise on 500 VBVR-Pro-Bench instances: give coding agents and video models the same first frame, the same natural-language instruction, the same output format and the same rule-based evaluator, and let the agents write programs to render the answer video instead of generating pixels. Codex (gpt-6-astra) scored 0.923, Claude Code (Fable 5.1) 0.894 and Gemini CLI (Gemini 3.1 Pro) 0.893, all above the strongest video model, VBVR-Pro-Wan2.2-I2V-A14B (RL), at 0.670. Best open-weight agent GLM-5 reached 0.572. Closed agents led in all five cognitive categories, with their largest edge in Abstraction (0.964 vs 0.741) and Perception (0.942 vs 0.488). Agents ran one attempt in a CPU-only container with a 30-minute cap, no ground truth and no image or video generation calls.
items.impact: It is a concrete data point for 'code as the reasoning interface': when a task has recoverable rules, a program is a more reliable answer medium than pixels. That logic carries over to agentic workflows where a script is both the rationale and the deliverable. But the benchmark is synthetic by construction - flat colours, exact geometry, deterministic checks - and the comparison is asymmetric: agents got tools, a sandbox and up to 30 minutes while video models produced a single sample. Token cost also varied by more than 10x among the near-tied closed agents.

items.title: MCP Reference Servers Patch Eight Vulnerabilities, Including Git LFS Code Execution
items.source: Model Context Protocol servers v2.6.0 release (Nov 27)
items.summary: The official MCP servers release fixes eight vulnerabilities across three servers and completes two partial fixes from v2.5.0. In mcp-server-git, Git LFS could execute programs named by a repository's own .git/config (GHSA-6663-fm5v-gqm5) from read-only tools such as git_status and git_diff; a crafted --repository root or objects/info/alternates could redirect reads to another repository; a tab in a remote name or a prefixed URL bypassed credential redaction; GitPython expanded $NAME in repo_path and leaked the value in errors; and git_merge could overwrite ignored files such as .env. server-memory fixed a symlink race that could chmod a file outside the memory path, and server-fetch extended robots.txt checks to backslash and path-parameter spellings. Windows filesystem listing gets a before-and-after junction check, though a swap-and-undo during the read is still missed. Upgrades: mcp-server-git and mcp-server-fetch to 2026.11.27, server-memory to 2.2.2, server-filesystem (Windows) to 2.4.1.
items.impact: MCP is turning into shared infrastructure for agents - Google made it the only supported path into Workspace yesterday - so weaknesses in reference servers are supply-chain issues, not toy bugs. The Git LFS and remote-name cases are especially relevant to coding agents that read untrusted repos. Note the version trap: npm package managers rank 2.2.2 and 2.4.1 below the old 2025.x/2026.x date versions, so those two must be installed explicitly.

items.title: Robots' Last Exam Opens: Nine Frontier Models Score Zero Once Given a Robot Body
items.summary: RLE went public on Nov 28 with ten reconstructed workplaces and a first wave of eight scenarios covering 16 complete paid-workflows such as making milk tea, pulling espresso and scanning items at checkout. Models get a job description, not step-by-step instructions, and are graded on the delivered artefact. In Agent Mode, where two floating grippers and a movable camera remove joint constraints, Claude Fable 5.2 finished 5 of 16 workflows (31.25%), Opus 5.5 two and GPT-6.2 Astra one; in 80 isolated subtasks Opus 5.5 passed 48.75%. In Embodied Mode, the same nine models driving a simulated Astribot S1 mobile dual-arm robot completed none of the 16 workflows. Fable's agent-mode successes were expensive: about five hours and ~54 million input tokens per workflow, with 38% of tool requests spent on coding and file operations versus 0% for most rivals. Sim-to-real checks on pouring, whiteboard wiping and bag lifting transferred a fixed code-as-policy from simulation to an ARX dual-arm at 85.6% success, 8-13 points below sim.
items.impact: This is the cleanest public evidence yet that strong workspace reasoning does not survive contact with kinematic constraints and error accumulation across a long workflow - small physics mistakes compound into failed delivery. The sim-real correlation work matters too: it gives the benchmark a reality check most simulation suites lack. Tests depend on final-state verification and reference agents prove each workflow solvable, but the task set is still small and community-built expansion is just starting.

items.title: MIT's PEAR Trains a Robot-Use Agent in Simulation Only, Then Runs It Zero-Shot on Hardware
items.source: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots (surfaced Nov 28)
items.summary: Song Han's MIT team introduced the Robot-Use Agent paradigm: a model sees three camera feeds plus arm state, writes a chain of thought, then emits a JSON end-effector pose that inverse kinematics executes - with no perception tools, motion planner or skill library in between. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B, pure reinforcement learning with task success as the only reward (no SFT, no demos) took LIBERO from 1.6% to 74.4%, LIBERO-Pro task swaps to 57.4% where pi0.5 drops from 96.9% to 0.75%, and previously unseen RoboLab-120 from 5.4% to 37.3%. On a real dual-arm YAM setup it went from 0/30 to 18/30 trials after simulation-only training. The training engine, built on veRL, LMCache, vLLM and Ray, is Apache-2.0 with weights released; nine general benchmarks showed no measurable capability loss.
items.impact: It points to an alternative to imitation-heavy VLA policies: teach a general reasoning model to 'use' a robot the way it uses a computer, and reuse normal post-training infrastructure. The instruction-following gain over pi0.5 is the most informative number in the paper. The costs are real, though - roughly 50,000 H100-equivalent GPU hours, ~3.2k thinking tokens per step (~4.3s even on fast hardware), 30 real trials on two task types, and 22.5 points below pi0.5 inside its training distribution.
